chunks: "They measure different things and fail in opposite ways, which is exactly why they are used together.
An accelerometer measures specific force, so at rest it reads gravity, and that gives me an absolute tilt reference that never drifts. But it also reads any real acceleration.
If the device is a car accelerating at 0. 3 g, the accelerometer thinks it is tilted by about 17 degrees. It is also noisy sample to sample.
So it is trustworthy at low frequencies, on average over seconds, and not trustworthy during motion. A gyroscope measures rotation rate.
It is smooth, has low noise, and responds instantly, so for short times integrating it gives an excellent angle.
But every gyro has a bias, and integrating a constant bias gives an error that grows linearly forever. Half a degree per second is 30 degrees after a minute.
So it is trustworthy at high frequencies and not at low ones.
Put them together with a complementary filter: take the gyro for fast changes, and let the accelerometer slowly pull the estimate back to gravity.
That is angle equals alpha times, the previous angle plus gyro times dt, plus one minus alpha times the accelerometer angle. With alpha 0.
98 at 100 hertz the time constant is half a second.
One more difference: neither can measure yaw drift when level, because gravity does not change when you rotate about the vertical. For heading you add a magnetometer or GPS."
